metadata.title: Literacy and Numeracy Proficiency in IALS, ALL and PIAAC (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The paper uses OECD ILSA/PIAAC adult literacy and numeracy assessments (IALS 1994-1998, ALL 2003-2007, PIAAC 2012) and compares proficiency across survey waves and countries. The analyses rely on OECD scaling/score estimation based on Item Response Theory (IRT) and on regression models that include demographic and education covariates; however, the excerpt does not specify whether the authors applied student/sampling weights or replicate weights from the microdata. For analysts working with the underlying datasets, complex survey weights are typically required to produce population-representative estimates and correct standard errors under the multistage sampling design. Because the manuscript excerpt does not report weight variable names or replicate design methods, the safest interpretation is that weighting/variance estimation follows OECD’s standard PIAAC/IALS/ALL public-data procedures, but this cannot be confirmed from the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a cross-survey comparability and descriptive/proficiency-change analysis using IRT-based proficiency scores rather than a PV-based achievement prediction task. The paper discusses item-level missingness and “not reached” responses for robustness checks, but it does not report a formal missing-data handling strategy for any student-level analytic dataset (e.g., imputation or deletion rules). Therefore, missing-data handling is treated as not reported because the excerpt does not document how missingness in covariates or responses was handled in the regression/estimation workflow.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper compares adult literacy proficiency across IALS (1994-1998), ALL (2003-2007), and PIAAC (2012) for countries/entities that participated in the relevant survey waves. For subgroup analyses, it restricts some comparisons to native-born respondents (explicitly stated for age-by-education and cohort analyses) to net out immigration composition effects. For cohort tracking, it selects individuals in the three oldest PIAAC age groups (35-44, 45-54, 55-65) and maps them back to the age group they belonged to at the time their country participated in IALS. For item-level robustness, it focuses on linking items common across IALS and PIAAC (nine common items, with further restrictions to those administered to representative samples across paper-based and computer-based modes), and it uses item-level definitions of missing vs not reached based on booklet administration rules.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD paper examines changes in adult literacy and numeracy proficiency across three large-scale assessments: IALS (1994-1998), ALL (2003-2007), and PIAAC (2012). It reports that literacy changes between IALS and PIAAC are often small to modest (e.g., several countries within about ±5 score points), while numeracy declines from ALL to PIAAC in most countries except Italy. The paper decomposes observed changes into (i) compositional shifts in age, education, and foreign-born shares and (ii) within-group proficiency changes, finding that composition effects generally cancel out and that most variation is attributable to within-group changes by age and educational attainment. It also conducts an item-level robustness analysis for literacy comparability between IALS and PIAAC, using linking items and examining missing vs “not reached” patterns and coding inconsistencies, with particular caution flagged for Italy and Poland. Finally, it evaluates the potential impact of PIAAC’s computer-based delivery using field-test evidence and concludes there is little evidence of a delivery-mode effect on literacy changes, though the paper urges caution due to cross-country implementation and technical comparability uncertainties.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is not an empirical ML prediction study; it is an OECD comparability and proficiency-change analysis using IRT-based proficiency scores and regression-style netting-out of compositional effects. As a result, there are no ML algorithms to extract, no PV-handling workflow, and no ML target-variable prediction metrics. The excerpt also does not provide microdata sample sizes (total N or per-country N), so those fields remain null despite the paper naming multiple countries/entities.
